title: Canada policy-influence network: McKinsey, WEF, immigration, and PRC interference
summary: Public-source research pass separating McKinsey/WEF policy-network and administrative influence, Canadian immigration-policy networks, and documented PRC foreign-interference mechanisms without collapsing those relationships into a control claim.

sources.title: Advisory Council on Economic Growth — Ideas into Action
IRCC opening remarks on McKinsey contracts
Auditor General — Professional Services Contracts / McKinsey
sources.publisher: Office of the Auditor General of Canada

sources.title: Global Affairs Canada foreign-affairs briefing book — World Economic Forum

caveats: Network relationships do not establish command-and-control.
McKinsey research or consulting does not by itself establish sovereign policy authority.
China-related professional ties do not establish CCP direction or foreign interference.
Several historical roster and relationship dates require deeper archival resolution.

provenance.method: public-source network research with evidence-category separation

classification_rules: Record WEF Strategic Partner, trustee, YGL, council, contributor, publication, event, and project relationships as distinct edge types.
Do not infer policy command or corruption from consulting, funding, event, or professional-network relationships alone.
Separate advisory recommendation from later policy adoption unless a primary source establishes the implementation pathway.
Treat PRC foreign interference as a distinct state-directed track and do not infer CCP direction from ordinary China-related ties.
Preserve counterevidence and unresolved chronology rather than forcing a control narrative.
data.method: Primary-source-first review of Canadian government, parliamentary, WEF, McKinsey, Century Initiative, and Foreign Interference Commission material; graph-edge enumeration; explicit evidentiary separation of institutional influence and covert foreign interference.
data.research_question: What documented McKinsey, WEF, immigration-policy, and PRC foreign-interference relationships shape or attempt to shape Canadian government institutions and policy processes?

findings.finding: McKinsey is formally listed as a WEF Strategic Partner and multiple current McKinsey board members have specific documented WEF roles or contributor footprints.
Century Initiative has direct personnel and project links to McKinsey, including historical Barton/Pickersgill board roles and a CI-McKinsey immigrant-integration report.

ACEG, chaired by Dominic Barton and supported by a pro-bono McKinsey research secretariat, recommended a 450,000 annual permanent-immigration trajectory and later described implementation of several associated reforms.

IRCC documented approximately $27.7 million in McKinsey transformation work covering strategy, roadmaps, operating models, digital services, processing improvements, and organizational transformation.
The Auditor General documented 97 McKinsey contracts worth $209 million in the audited federal/Crown population for 2011–2023 and significant procurement-policy failures.
Canadian official assessments describe the PRC as the most active foreign-interference actor targeting Canada; this is analytically separate from WEF/McKinsey institutional-network influence.

No reviewed evidence establishes literal WEF or McKinsey command-and-control over the Canadian government, and the Foreign Interference Commission did not find PRC interference determined overall federal election outcomes.
